comments.content: This is a regression. Before this change, the route returned `errors` and `devices` without touching Sheet1. Now, when any TV has an open incident and `fetchSheet1Data()` rejects (Graph/Excel outage or timeout), the whole request goes to `shapeError`. The customer window then loses its existing errors and devices lists, and it happens exactly when the customer has a problem. `silenced` only changes the wording of the status line, so it should degrade gracefully. If the Sheet1 read fails, fall back to `silenced = false` (or log the failure) and still return the rest of the payload. `live-actions.ts` already handles a 'graph down' case in a similar way.
comments.existing_code:
const [watchMember, customers] = await Promise.all([getWatchMember(db, member.userId), fetchSheet1Data()]);
      silenced = watchCustomer(watchMember, sheetByClientNumber(customers), now).silenced;

comments.content: If Sheet1 can't be read, the whole "Can't watch now" list turns into an error, even though the incidents were already loaded from the DB. Sheet1 is only used to drop silenced customers and to add names to labels. Falling back to an empty map shows every open incident unsilenced, labelled by email. That fails safe, so Kevin still sees real outages during an Excel/Graph outage.

`formatStamp` is now exported from this file, but `src/components/admin/live-errors-view.tsx` still has its own copy at line 51. The new `WatchProblems` table uses that local copy. That makes two identical copies of the "dd/mm/yyyy hh:mm" formatter. Move it to `@/lib/utils` next to `formatDate`, and import it in both places so they can't drift apart.

This client component imports a type from a server route module. That route imports `getAdminPool`, `requireOperator` and `fetchSheet1Data`. `import type` is erased at build time, so this is safe today. But if someone later turns it into a value import, server-only code ends up in the client bundle. Move `WatchProblem` to a shared types file (for example `src/lib/watch-customers.ts` or a `types` module), and import it from there in both the route and this view.

The 24-hour cut-off and the alert query use different timestamps. The cut-off here uses `q.receivedAt`, which a merge moves to now. The incident is stored with `started_at = q.firstReceivedAt`, and `toAlert` only picks incidents with `started_at > now - 24h`.

Suppose a failure row was first received more than 24 h ago and the TV is still failing, so the row keeps merging. It passes this check and an incident opens, but that incident never qualifies for `toAlert`. It also appears on the screens with an old `started_at`, and grey once 7 days have passed. The result is an incident that is never alerted, while every later run skips this TV because an incident is already open. Use the same timestamp in both places: either run the cut-off on `firstReceivedAt`, or store `started_at` from the same field the cut-off uses.

An `instanceof pg.Pool` check is fragile when Next bundles the app with a workspace package. `getAdminPool()` builds its Pool from the app's `pg` import. If that is a different `pg` module instance from core's, this check is false for a real Pool. The function then runs `pg_advisory_xact_lock` in autocommit, so the lock is released straight away, and each step runs as its own query on whatever pooled connection it gets. You lose both atomicity and mutual exclusion without any error. Use duck typing instead, e.g. `typeof (db as Pool).connect === 'function' && !('release' in db)`, or make the caller pass an explicit flag.

`last_play_at` is overwritten unconditionally. A play note that is retried or arrives late with an older TV time moves `last_play_at` backwards. Step (b) filters failures with `e.last_at > d.last_play_at`, so failures that a newer play had already superseded count again and can reopen an incident. Use `greatest(public.live_device.last_play_at, excluded.last_play_at)`, and update `last_play_proxy` only when the note is the newer one. This also needs the matching change in schema.sql.

`rowBlocked` returns true for an expiry date that can't be parsed. In that case this branch still calls `formatDate`, which has no NaN guard, so the line reads "Subscription ended NaN/NaN/NaN". There is a second problem: `rowBlocked` compares UTC days, but `formatDate` uses the browser's local day. West of UTC, an expiry at midnight UTC shows the day before the one the rule used. Only add the date when it parses, and format it from its UTC parts.

`i.customer` comes from `watchCustomer().label`, which already ends with "(client N)" or "(clients A, B)" whenever the member has client numbers. So the Clients column repeats what the Customer cell already shows. Either drop this column, or send a label without the numbers from the route.

`runWatchCheck` holds `pg_advisory_xact_lock` only until its transaction commits. All Telegram sends and `markAlerted`/`markClearAlerted` calls happen after that, outside the lock. If a second run starts while the first is still sending (a manual POST or curl retry, or a slow run of up to 10 s per message plus the Sheet1 fetch overlapping the next timer tick), it reads the same `toAlert`/`toClearAlert` rows and sends the same messages again. The `alerted_at is null` guard in `markAlerted` stops a second stamp, but the duplicate message has already gone out. Options: take a session-level advisory lock (`pg_try_advisory_lock`) around the whole route and return early if it is held, or claim rows inside the transaction before sending (for example a `sending_at` column or `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`).
comments.existing_code: const run = await runWatchCheck(pool, { now, fixedCodes: codes.fixed });

comments.content: If `fetchSheet1Data()` throws, the route returns 500 and sends nothing, including "watching again" messages and alerts that don't depend on silencing. `toAlert` only includes incidents with `started_at` in the last 24 h. So if Sheet1 or Graph stays down for about a day, those can't-watch alerts drop out of `toAlert` without ever being sent. Consider catching the error here and falling back to an empty sheet with silencing turned off, so customers are labelled by email and alerts still go out. Note that an empty map can't simply be passed in: `vpsProxyBlock(undefined)` returns "cancelled", which would silence everyone.

Every failure is reported as a retryable `"failed"`, including permanent 400s such as "message is too long". The texts are not capped at Telegram's 4096-character limit. A provider-down batch with many customer labels, or a multi-TV alert where each line carries the long 513 advice, could go over it. Such an alert would then be retried every 5 minutes until it ages out after 24 h and is lost. A `kind: "clear"` message has no age cut-off in `toClearAlert`, so it would be retried forever and keep that user's clear pending. Consider truncating or splitting texts in `planWatchMessages`, and logging 4xx results (other than 429) differently from transient errors.

This repeats the `SITE` constant and the `/members?member=` link format from `watch-customers.ts`. Export one helper from `watch-customers.ts` (for example `fallbackWatchCustomer(userId)`) and reuse it here, so the two can't drift apart.

`qualifyingFailure` looks at every counting failure since the last play, with no age limit, and the 24-hour cut-off only runs after it has picked one row. If a TV has an old qualifying row and no play since, that row is always picked. Examples: a blocking `account_expired` from 3 days ago, or a row with `repeat_count` of 2 or more from last week. The cut-off then skips the TV, and newer failures from today are never considered. That TV can't open an incident until it plays again, so a customer who is failing right now gets no alert. Drop rows older than the cut-off before choosing the qualifying row, e.g. `counting.filter(f => nowMs - Date.parse(f.receivedAt) < CUTOFF_MS)`. Or bound `failuresAfterPlay` by `received_at` for step (b).

This match is too broad. If `grant kevbox_admin to postgres` fails (the script only prints a note when it does), `set role kevbox_admin` fails with `permission denied to set role "kevbox_admin"`. That also contains `permission denied`, so the check reports PASS even though the DELETE never ran as kevbox_admin. Match the table-level error instead.
comments.suggestion_code:
elif grep -q 'permission denied for table live_watch_incident' "$WORK/del.err"; then
  pass "kevbox_admin cannot delete from live_watch_incident (permission denied)"
comments.existing_code:
elif grep -q 'permission denied' "$WORK/del.err"; then
  pass "kevbox_admin cannot delete from live_watch_incident (permission denied)"

comments.content: The header says the script proves AC-32's server merge, but no check runs `record_live_errors_as`. 0016 rewrites that function in two ways: a merge takes the newest entry's `proxy`, keeping the stored flag when the entry's flag is null or older, and a merge must not move `first_received_at`. The script only hashes the function and checks that A cannot execute it. Add a postgres-side check: insert an entry with proxy=false, merge a later entry with proxy=true and assert proxy=true; merge an older entry with proxy=false and assert proxy stays true; merge an entry with proxy null and assert proxy stays true; assert `first_received_at` is unchanged and `received_at` moved. Without that check, drop AC-32 from the header.
comments.existing_code: # prove-live-watch.sh — proves migration 0016 (AC-9, AC-10, AC-11, AC-32's server merge) on a LOCAL

comments.content: `-hmac "$JWT_SECRET"` (and the `curl -H "...: $SERVICE_ROLE_KEY"` calls) put the secret in the process's argv, where `ps` on the host can see it. The header says the script never exposes these values. For local demo keys this matters little, but if the promise should hold, use `openssl mac -macopt hexkey:...` with input from a file, or a short `python3` HMAC that reads the secret from the environment. Pass curl headers through `-H @file`.

The two batching rules pick the host in different ways. Can't-watch batching uses the host of each customer's *earliest* incident (`s.incidents[0].providerHost` in `providerBatches`). Watching-again batching uses the host of the incident that cleared *last*. It also has no 15-minute window, unlike the alert side. So a customer with TVs on two hosts can be counted under host X in the "N customers… all on X" alert and under host Y in the matching "N customers on Y are watching again" message. Customers who cleared far apart (for example after a Telegram outage) can also end up in one combined message. Use the same host choice for both, and if the spec intends it, the same time window too.

The local-host guard can be bypassed for DB_URL because `url_host` and libpq split the URL differently. `url_host` cuts at the first `/`, `?` or `#` before it removes the `user@` part. libpq's URI parser looks only for `@` or `/` when it finds user info. Take `postgresql://127.0.0.1?@evil.example/postgres` or `postgresql://127.0.0.1#@evil.example/postgres`. The script reads the host as `127.0.0.1`. The query-string check doesn't catch them either, because `db_query` is `@evil.example/postgres`, with no `host=` and no `%`. libpq, though, treats `127.0.0.1?` as the user name and connects to `evil.example`. The `db_authority` comma check has the same weakness, since it also cuts at `?` and `#`. Fix: for DB_URL, find the authority the way libpq does. Cut only at the first `/`, then take the text after the last `@`, and refuse it if any `?` or `#` remains.
comments.suggestion_code:
url_host() {
  local rest="${1#*://}"
  rest="${rest%%/*}"      # libpq: authority ends at the first '/'
  rest="${rest##*@}"      # user info ends at the last '@' before it
  [[ "$rest" == *[?#]* ]] && { printf '%s' "$rest"; return; }  # never a plain local host
  printf '%s' "${rest%%:*}"
}
